data: {"type":"agent_chunk","agent":"synthesizer","content":"## Overview

CRISPR gene editing is a genetic engineering technique that modifies the genomes of living organisms. It is based on a simplified version of the bacterial CRISPR-Cas9 antiviral defense system [1]. In bacteria, CRISPR sequences derive from bacteriophage DNA and detect and destroy DNA from similar phages during later infections [2].

## How It Works

- **Targeted cutting:** Delivering Cas9 nuclease with a synthetic guide RNA (gRNA) into a cell lets the genome be cut at a chosen location, so genes can be removed or new ones added [1].
- **Repair and outcome:** Cas9 is a DNA-cutting endonuclease that makes site-specific double-stranded breaks [3]. Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) repair supports gene inactivation and removal [3]. Precise insertion generally requires homology-directed repair instead, because NHEJ is error-prone. The source's grouping of insertion under NHEJ is therefore imprecise.

## Where It Is Used

The CRISPR-Cas9 system is widely used in genetic engineering, medicine, agriculture, and biotechnology [3]. The research does not give specific examples within these fields.

## Caveats

- The targeting claim and the broad-application claim each rest on a single source, so treat them as provisional.
- The research omits off-target cutting, where Cas9 cuts unintended sites, and the ethical limits on editing. Both are central to medical and agricultural use.

### Sources

1. [CRISPR gene editing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CRISPR_gene_editing) - Wikipedia
2. [CRISPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CRISPR) - Wikipedia
3. [Cas9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cas9) - Wikipedia
